name: Betz's Law
statement: No wind turbine can extract more than about three-fifths of the energy in the wind passing through it.
statementAccent: more than about three-fifths of the energy
meaning: Betz's law states that no open, free-stream wind turbine can capture more than about fifty-nine percent of the kinetic energy in the wind passing through its rotor. The precise maximum, the Betz limit, is sixteen twenty-sevenths of the incoming wind power, roughly zero point five nine three. The reason is intuitive: if a turbine could extract all the wind's energy, the air behind it would stop completely and block the flow, so to keep air moving through, the wind must retain some speed downstream, and only a fraction of its energy can be harvested. Derived by Albert Betz in 1919 from basic fluid mechanics, the law sets the theoretical ceiling on the aerodynamic efficiency of wind turbines and is a foundational result of wind-energy engineering.
mechanism: Betz modelled the turbine as an idealised actuator disk that slows the wind, and applied conservation of mass and momentum to the air passing through. Slowing the wind extracts energy, but slowing it too much chokes the flow, since the same air must continue downstream; there is an optimum amount of slowing. The analysis shows the power extracted is maximised when the turbine reduces the wind to one-third of its upstream speed, and at that optimum the fraction of the incoming kinetic energy captured is exactly sixteen twenty-sevenths. This limit follows purely from the physics of an ideal fluid and applies to any open-flow turbine regardless of its design, so no rotor spinning in the free wind can beat it.

examples.text: Maximum power is captured when the turbine slows the wind to one-third of its upstream speed; slowing it more chokes the flow and slowing it less wastes energy.
Modern large wind turbines reach power coefficients of roughly zero point four five to zero point five, about three-quarters to four-fifths of the Betz limit, never exceeding it.
The limit was derived independently by Frederick Lanchester and Nikolay Zhukovsky as well as Betz, a classic instance of the same result found by several people.

variants.name: The actuator-disk model
variants.text: The idealisation treating the rotor as a thin disk that slows the flow, from which the Betz limit is derived using conservation of mass and momentum.

variants.name: Ducted turbines
variants.text: Shrouded or diffuser-augmented turbines that channel extra flow through the rotor and so can exceed the limit relative to the bare rotor area, though not the total device area.

whyItMatters: Betz's law sets the fundamental efficiency ceiling for wind power, telling engineers that even a perfect turbine can harvest at most about fifty-nine percent of the wind's kinetic energy. It frames the whole enterprise of turbine design, which aims to approach but can never surpass the limit, and it explains why real turbines, achieving three-quarters or so of it, are already close to the physical best.

working.text: expect no open-flow turbine to capture more than sixteen twenty-sevenths, about fifty-nine percent, of the wind's kinetic energy.
design toward slowing the wind to about one-third of its upstream speed, the condition that maximises extracted power.
compare a turbine's power coefficient to the Betz limit; reaching three-quarters of it is already excellent, and exceeding it is impossible for a bare rotor.

limits: The limit applies to open, free-stream turbines modelled as an ideal actuator disk; ducted or shrouded turbines that channel extra air can exceed it relative to the bare rotor area, though not relative to the whole device's cross-section. The derivation assumes an ideal, incompressible, inviscid fluid and ignores real losses from blade drag, tip vortices, finite blade count, and wake rotation, so actual turbines fall well below the limit, reaching perhaps three-quarters of it. The law bounds aerodynamic capture of kinetic energy at the rotor, not the overall system efficiency, which further losses in gearboxes and generators reduce.
misreadings: The fifty-nine percent is of the kinetic energy in the wind passing through the rotor, not of some other total or of all the wind in the sky. The limit is not violated by real turbines, which operate below it; claims of exceeding it usually involve ducted designs measured against the bare rotor area rather than the full device. And Betz's law caps aerodynamic capture at the rotor, not the whole turbine's output, which additional mechanical and electrical losses reduce further, so the limit is a ceiling on one stage, not a promise of near-sixty-percent electricity.
origin: Formulated by the German physicist Albert Betz in 1919 using actuator-disk momentum theory, and derived independently by Frederick Lanchester around 1915 and Nikolay Zhukovsky around 1920.
